case_study_insert.main_stem: Lumen River Cruises (LCU) is a public limited company in the tourism sector, operating river cruises and employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 1998 by Elena Lumen, the company has a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. LCU plans to invest $1,200,000 in two new river cruise boats, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $550,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $165, and produces 12,000 units a year, where each unit is one passenger-cruise place. LCU faces a 6% cancellation rate and rising complaints about cabin cleanliness from corporate charter groups during the peak season.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Guest Services Report — Q2 2025: LCU sold 6,800 passenger-cruise places, with a 6% cancellation rate. Cabin-cleanliness complaints reached 27, up from 18 last year, and average boarding took 35 minutes. A survey of 1,800 passengers gave LCU a 4.4/5 rating, and 61% said they would recommend the cruise. Catering waste was 9% of meals prepared. A skills audit shows 18 of 95 crew have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the maritime academy costs $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Lumen River Cruises as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.58 to $13.40 an hour, raising crew payroll. (3) Marine fuel and port charges have risen 14.0% year-on-year, while inbound tourism bookings grew 7.3%.

questions.question_text: LCU is raising $1,200,000 for two new river cruise boats through a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for LCU of the share issue compared with the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue provides $500,000 with no interest charge and no obligation to repay, so LCU can devote more of the $165 selling price to covering the $550,000 fixed costs and the $55 variable cost per passenger-cruise place. Unlike the $700,000 bank loan, equity does not require collateral, protecting the two new boats from repossession if the 6% cancellation rate worsens.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the $1,200,000 funding between lenders and shareholders, leaving borrowing capacity for future needs such as the 27 cabin-cleanliness complaints and the $1,100 per crew training. As a public limited company, LCU can reach investors more easily than a smaller firm, and the 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers and 61% who would recommend the cruise make the shares attractive. Existing shareholders dilute their claim, but no fixed repayment schedule strains cash flow during the peak season. The 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers and the 61% recommendation rate reduce the risk that new investors demand an immediate return.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to LCU's fleet expansion financing.

questions.question_text: LCU wants to fill its two new river cruise boats. Consider a national television campaign, travel trade fairs, or social media influencer marketing. Which should LCU choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television: TV would showcase the river scenery to millions and help fill 12,000 passenger-cruise places quickly, supporting the 7.3% growth in inbound tourism bookings. Yet airtime is very expensive on top of $550,000 fixed costs and a $700,000 loan, and many viewers will not cruise, so much of the budget is wasted.

Travel trade fairs: Fairs put LCU directly in front of tour operators and corporate charter groups, the very customers behind the cabin-cleanliness complaints, and allow face-to-face selling of group bookings. They are cheaper than TV but geographically limited, staff-intensive, and may not reach the independent travellers who gave the 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel vloggers can show cabins, boarding and the river experience to a global audience, with the 4.4/5 rating and 61% recommendation rate providing credible content. Engagement is measurable against the 6,800 places already sold and the 6% cancellation rate, though results take time and depend on influencer credibility, and the 35-minute boarding issue must be fixed before inviting scrutiny.

Recommendation: LCU should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by selective trade-fair attendance for corporate charters. It reaches both leisure and group buyers far more widely than fairs and at far lower cost than television, while converting the strong passenger rating into bookings for the $1,200,000 boats. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a company servicing a $700,000 loan, and trade fairs alone are rejected as too narrow to fill two new boats. The 35-minute boarding issue should be fixed first so influencers show a high-quality experience to potential passengers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to LCU.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of LCU with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and trade fairs are rejected.

questions.question_text: LCU's cancellation rate has reached 6% and cabin-cleanliness complaints are rising among its workforce of 95. Explain two benefits for LCU of introducing quality circles.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles bring small groups of cabin and onboard staff together regularly to identify causes of the 27 cleanliness complaints and propose fixes, using the knowledge of the workforce of 95 who clean and inspect the cabins daily. This prevention-focused approach should reduce complaints from the 18 recorded last year, protecting the 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers and the 61% who would recommend LCU.

Point 2: Because staff help design the solution under LCU's democratic leadership, they are more committed to carrying it out, which can shorten the 35-minute boarding process and reduce the 6% cancellation rate from corporate charter groups. Fewer cancellations mean more of the 12,000 passenger-cruise places are sold at $165, protecting the $110 contribution needed to cover $550,000 fixed costs and service the $700,000 bank loan. Under democratic leadership, quality-circle suggestions are more likely to be implemented, cutting the 9% catering waste as well as the 27 cleanliness complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LCU's complaints, cancellations, rating and costs.

questions.question_text: LCU must train 18 of 95 crew who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the maritime academy. Which should LCU choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on board is specific to LCU's own cleaning standards and boarding routine, costs no course fees, and keeps the 18 trainees working during cruises. It can tackle the 27 cabin-cleanliness complaints immediately and help reduce the 35-minute boarding time. The drawbacks are that senior crew teaching on board have less time for their own duties, bad habits can be copied, and there is no formal certificate for a public limited company that markets quality to charter groups.

Off-the-job training: The maritime academy course at $1,100 per employee gives structured, certified hospitality and safety skills. For 18 staff the stated fee is 18 × $1,100 = $19,800, affordable beside the $1,200,000 fleet investment. However, it removes 18 of 95 crew from service, which could worsen the 6% cancellation rate during the peak season, and generic content still needs on-site adaptation to LCU's cabins.

Decision: LCU should choose on-the-job training as the priority, with certified academy modules afterwards for senior crew. It is cheaper, tailored to the actual boats and avoids losing 18 crew from a workforce of 95 at the busiest time. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the $19,800 fee and lost shifts would undermine the drive to cut 27 complaints and 6% cancellations, and quality standards must be consistent on the two new boats from launch. Elena Lumen should pilot the on-the-job approach on one boat, tracking the 27 complaints and 35-minute boarding time before deciding whether the $19,800 academy route is justified for all 18 crew.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to LCU.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of LCU.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, service disruption and standards relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how LCU's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Labour productivity = Output ÷ Number of workers. Substitution: 12,000 ÷ 95 = 126.32 passenger-cruise places per worker. Answer: labour productivity is 126.32 units per worker.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $165 − $55 = $110. Answer: contribution per unit is $110.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways LCU's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Labour productivity of 126.32 places per worker lets managers monitor the workforce of 95 as two new boats are added, setting crew targets so the 6% cancellation rate does not rise.
2. Break-even is $550,000 ÷ $110 = 5,000 places, so with 12,000 places the margin of safety is 7,000, a cushion that justifies the $1,200,000 fleet investment to shareholders.
3. Contribution of $110 allows pricing tests: a $15 discount to $150 leaves $95 contribution, so managers can judge whether filling cabins for corporate charters offsets the loss while addressing 27 cleanliness complaints.
4. Managers can track unit cost, $550,000 ÷ 12,000 = $45.83 plus $55 variable cost = $100.83 a place, against the 14.0% rise in marine fuel to decide whether to raise the $165 price or improve the 9% catering-waste rate.

questions.model_answer: (i) Labour productivity = 126.32 places per worker | (ii) Contribution per unit = $110 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: productivity of 126.32 for 95 crew; break-even 5,000 and 7,000 margin of safety; $110 contribution for charter discount decisions; and unit-cost benchmarking at $100.83 against 14.0% fuel inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LCU's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LCU's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.53 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.19 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $120,000 + $70,000 = $245,000. For 2024, $195,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.30 and ($195,000 − $60,000) ÷ $150,000 = $135,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.90. For 2025, $245,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.53 and ($245,000 − $55,000) ÷ $160,000 = $190,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.19.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened clearly. The first ratio rose from 1.30 to 1.53 even though current liabilities increased from $150,000 to $160,000, because cash almost doubled from $40,000 to $70,000. The second measure improved from 0.90 to 1.19, showing LCU can now cover short-term obligations without relying on its $55,000 of inventories, valuable while it services a $700,000 bank loan and invests $1,200,000 in two boats. The qualification is trade receivables, up from $95,000 to $120,000: if corporate charter groups pay late, the stronger ratios could quickly weaken, and the 6% cancellation rate also threatens cash inflow.

Conclusion: LCU's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement is not dependent on stock, so short-term solvency is healthier. The main residual risk is the rise in receivables, so credit control and deposit terms for charters should be tightened before further expansion. Larger deposits would also reduce the receivables balance and make the improvement more durable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: LCU is considering a flexible cancellation policy to reduce its 6% cancellation rate. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LCU of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Allowing free date changes rather than lost deposits can persuade corporate charter groups to move a booking instead of cancelling, directly cutting the 6% cancellation rate. That protects the 12,000 passenger-cruise places and the $110 contribution, sustaining the 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers and the 61% recommendation rate while the two new boats are brought into service.

Disadvantage: Flexible terms shift risk to LCU: a late change may leave a cabin empty, and the $165 selling price may effectively fall if no fee is charged. With $550,000 fixed costs and a $700,000 loan, that reduces the contribution available per sailing. The insert gives no figure for how many cancellations would be converted, so the net benefit cannot be quantified and the policy should be judged cautiously. LCU should test the policy with corporate charter groups first, since the 27 cleanliness complaints and the 35-minute boarding time may matter more to them than flexible terms.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LCU's cancellations, passenger rating and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.0% rise in marine fuel and port charges will affect LCU. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If LCU's $700,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000). That is a small fraction of $550,000 fixed costs, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. The rise could make the $500,000 share issue relatively more attractive and may trim some discretionary travel despite 7.3% growth in inbound bookings.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.40 an hour): LCU's workforce of 95 includes hourly-paid cabin and catering crew, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual pay, so any annual figure would be invented. The defensible measure is productivity: 12,000 units ÷ 95 staff = 126.32 passenger-cruise places per worker, so the higher wage is bearable only if that rate holds as two boats are added; quality circles and training the 18 untrained crew can support it.

Marine fuel and port charges (14.0%): These feed the $55 variable cost of each place. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only an upper bound is defensible: if the full $55 were exposed, 14.0% × $55 = $7.70 a unit, and at 12,000 units that is about $92,400 a year (12,000 × $7.70). Even a smaller exposed share cuts the $110 contribution on every place, and unlike the interest cost it recurs with each sailing.

Conclusion: The 14.0% rise in fuel and port charges will have the greatest impact. It compounds over 12,000 places and directly erodes the $110 contribution that services the $700,000 loan and supports the $1,200,000 boats, whereas the interest rise costs only $5,250 a year on the stated loan and the wage effect can be offset by maintaining 126.32 places per worker. LCU should review the $165 price and cut the 9% catering waste rather than absorb the full increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to LCU.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LCU's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that the fuel and port charge rise has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
